title: Questions of law, fact, and mixed application
shortTitle: Questions of law, fact, and mixed application
summary: A question of law asks what legal standard governs; a factual question asks what happened or what the evidence establishes; a mixed question applies a legal standard to facts. The boundary can affect how closely a court reviews agency action.
notes:
The distinction becomes especially consequential when legal interpretation receives independent review while factfinding and policy choices receive deferential review. Loper Bright’s majority characterizes Gray v. Powell and NLRB v. Hearst Publications as factbound applications within particular delegations. Kagan questions whether that characterization can separate them from much statutory interpretation, because applying a broad statutory category often defines its meaning. (Printed 942–943, 958–959, 965.)

The notes use John Dickinson’s 1927 analysis to challenge the idea of a fixed natural boundary. In his account, policy choices about judicial control can influence whether a court describes an issue as law or fact. This is an attributed scholarly criticism. It does not erase the governing review provisions, nor establish that every classification is arbitrary. It asks the reader to explain what the court is reviewing and why the assigned standard follows. (Printed 965–966.)

For study purposes, identify the disputed proposition before naming the review standard. Whether herring vessels must carry observers differs from whether the statute permits requiring payment. Whether an employee remained on call differs from how compensable time is defined and applied. Whether an agency has statutory power to regulate differs from whether its chosen policy is supported and reasonably explained. Skidmore, Loper Bright, and the historical Gray/Hearst discussion make these distinctions concrete. (Printed 930–932, 939–950.)
